questions.enonce_markdown: Make a large fully labeled drawing of the cross-section of the human eye. *[7 marks]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
**What the large drawing must show (horizontal section of the right eye, with label lines and the title "Cross-section of the human eye"):**

1. **Sclera** (white, tough outer coat) and, at the front, the transparent **cornea** (main refracting surface) covered by the **conjunctiva**.
2. **Choroid** (middle coat, dark pigmented, rich in blood vessels) continuing in front as the **ciliary body** (containing the **ciliary muscles**) and the **iris** with the **pupil** at its centre.
3. **Suspensory ligaments** joining the ciliary body to the **lens** (transparent, biconvex, held behind the iris).
4. **Aqueous humour** (watery fluid between the cornea and the lens) and **vitreous humour** (transparent jelly filling the large chamber behind the lens).
5. **Retina** (inner light-sensitive coat) with the **yellow spot (macula) and its centre, the fovea** (cones only, greatest visual acuity) on the optical axis, and the **blind spot** (no photoreceptors) where the **optic nerve** leaves the eye.
6. **Optic nerve** to the brain, and the **retinal blood vessels**.

**Marking guide:** large, neat outline with the correct shape (1); sclera, cornea, choroid, retina (2); iris, pupil, lens, ciliary body, suspensory ligaments (2); humours (1); fovea, blind spot, optic nerve (1).

questions.enonce_markdown:
Identify the problems involved in the following eye defects and their methods of correction:

(i) Long-sightedness (Hypermetropia).

(ii) Short-sightedness (Myopia). *[8 marks]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i) Long-sightedness (hypermetropia)**

- **Problem:** a person can see **distant objects clearly but not near objects**. The **eyeball is too short** (from front to back) or the **lens is too weak (too thin, cannot become convex enough)**, or the cornea is too flat, so the light rays from a near object are **focused behind the retina**. The image on the retina is blurred. It is common in older people (presbyopia) when the lens loses elasticity.
- **Correction:** wearing **spectacles or contact lenses with a convex (converging) lens**, which converges the rays before they enter the eye so that the image is formed on the retina. Laser surgery can also reshape the cornea.

**(ii) Short-sightedness (myopia)**

- **Problem:** a person can see **near objects clearly but not distant objects**. The **eyeball is too long** or the **lens is too strong (too thick and curved, cannot become thin enough)** or the cornea is too curved, so the rays from a distant object are **focused in front of the retina**; the image on the retina is blurred.
- **Correction:** wearing **spectacles or contact lenses with a concave (diverging) lens**, which spreads out the rays before they enter the eye so that the image falls on the retina. Laser surgery that flattens the cornea is another method.

**Ray diagrams expected (rewarded):** for each defect, one diagram of the uncorrected eye (image behind or in front of the retina) and one with the correcting lens (image on the retina).

questions.enonce_markdown: Explain the mechanism of color vision in humans. *[5 marks]* *(7, 8, 5 marks)*
questions.corrige_markdown:
Colour vision depends on the **cone cells** of the retina, which work in **bright light** and are concentrated in the **fovea**. It is explained by the **trichromatic theory** (Young-Helmholtz).

1. The retina contains **three types of cone cells**, each with a different **visual pigment (iodopsin)** that absorbs light best in a different part of the spectrum: **blue-sensitive cones** (maximum about 420 nm), **green-sensitive cones** (about 530 nm) and **red-sensitive cones** (about 560 nm).
2. When light falls on a cone, the pigment (a protein, **opsin**, combined with **retinal**) **absorbs a photon** and the retinal changes from the *cis* to the *trans* form; the pigment breaks down. This **changes the permeability of the cell membrane** and produces a **generator potential**, which leads to nerve impulses through the **bipolar cells** and **ganglion cells** into the **optic nerve**.
3. Light of one colour **stimulates the three cone types in different proportions**; the brain (**visual cortex**) **interprets the combination** of impulses as a particular colour. For example, red and green cones stimulated equally gives yellow; **equal stimulation of all three** gives white; no stimulation gives black.
4. If one type of cone is missing or defective, the person is **colour-blind** (e.g. red-green colour blindness, a sex-linked recessive condition).
